Pele Yoetz 88:1: Aggadah - This is one of the things that is beneficial as a means to restrain transgression and to bring sin to an end: when the sage sits and expounds words of Aggadah and says Kaddish, and they answer after him "Amen, yehei shemei rabba," the Holy One, blessed be He, forgives the sins of Israel - so said our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Shabbat 119b). And certainly this applies if he first regrets the past and accepts upon himself to strive not to return again to folly to do evil - "the LORD also has taken away your sin" and passes over transgression. And this too is necessary: that he hear the sermon with affection and answer "Amen, yehei shemei rabba" with intention, for then he gives great peace of mind to his Former, since our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 49a) that the world stands upon the Kaddish said after Aggadah. And even though we do not know how to direct our handiwork, may He establish it for us, and may the LORD also grant the good and command forgiveness. And therefore, throughout all the dispersions of Israel, it is customary to say after every oral Torah study "Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya," and so on, which is Aggadah, in order to say Kaddish over a matter of Aggadah.
Pele Yoetz 88:2: And behold, it is called "Aggadata" because it draws a person's heart, from the language of "and it was dragged (neged u'nefak) from before Him" (Daniel 7:10). And all words of Aggadah are full of arousal to fear and love the LORD. Go out and learn from this Aggadah which states (Makkot 23b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel, therefore He multiplied for them Torah and mitzvot - this is a great love and a great good beyond compare, and so too from every word of Aggadah a person shall find to learn from them ethics and fear of the LORD, if he sets his mind to them. And even in the puzzling Aggadot, our commentator Rabbis have already informed us that the plain meaning of them alone does not suffice, but rather our Rabbis, of blessed memory, intended by them a hint alluding to esoteric matters, besides that hidden within them are secrets of the Torah, and Aggadot are themselves secrets - and we have already heard a warning not to teach or state a puzzling Aggadah in the presence of an ignorant person, lest he think it is according to its plain meaning and come to mock the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, God forbid. And how good it is, when one teaches words of Aggadah in the presence of the multitude of the people, to also tell them the ethical lesson that emerges from it, for not every person sets his heart to understand one thing from within another.
Pele Yoetz 88:3: And especially in the reading of the Haggadah on Passover night, which is a Torah-mandated mitzvah, as it is written (Exodus 13:8), "and you shall tell your son." And whoever expands in telling of the Exodus from Egypt is praiseworthy. And the essence of the mitzvah is to tell his sons and his wife the acts of the LORD in fine detail and to increase telling His praise and His very capability and His individual providence, and the greatness of His love and His affection and His compassion, and how many good qualities He has shown toward us - and that therefore an obligation rests upon us to fear and love the Name and to serve Him with complete service - this is the entire fruit of the Haggadah.
Pele Yoetz 88:4: And since all the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, came in number and in weight, and hidden within them are concealed secrets, therefore it is fitting for every person to read each passage first in the holy tongue, and afterward explain it to the members of his household, and to intend that each word ascend upward and that the matters be repaired at their root in the upper place. And they extolled at length in the Holy Zohar the praise attaching to the telling of the Exodus from Egypt, and one who rejoices in that telling gives how much peace of mind before our Father in Heaven, and He shall repay him his reward. And this teaching of the Holy Zohar has already been printed in the prayer books at Parashat Bo, and it is fitting to take it to heart, to be aroused with joy to consider deeply how good is our portion and how pleasant is our lot, that such great and abundant love and affection is made known to us from our Father, our Shepherd, the King, high and exalted, whose greatness is beyond fathoming, and in what lies before us abundant affection is made known to us, that He sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to tell of the miracles He performed with us and made a remembrance for His wonders, and commanded us to eat matzah and maror, and so on - and every single thing and every single utterance, and especially our joy, bears fruit above and gives peace of mind to our Former, and He builds His chambers in heaven through us, what no hand of ours could otherwise reach, only we know that our handiwork He established for us, and the Holy One, blessed be He, fixes for us good reward for all of this. Is there any palate sweeter than this? Happy are we, how good is our portion - it is impossible not to rejoice. And granted that everything follows a person's deeds and the merit of his soul, so shall his soul be aroused to love and joy - but an obligation rests upon us to labor with thoughts and with external arousal to arouse love and joy, whether much or little as our hand attains, may the LORD be a help to us, for whoever comes to purify himself is assisted from Heaven (Shabbat 104a). (And more is written on this under the entry "Pesach.")
Pele Yoetz 88:5: And I have already stated that for everything, preparation beforehand is necessary, and care leads to diligence (Avodah Zarah 20b) - so too in this matter, one must make preparation beforehand so that he not be hungry and not become dulled during the year. And even the firstborns, who fast on the eve of Passover and for whom it is difficult, due to the fast, to lengthen the Haggadah, and it is not so possible for them to rejoice due to weakness of heart - in any case, the occasion requires strengthening oneself with much vigor and might, and let him do whatever is in his power to do, and drink coffee and good soup before the reading of the Haggadah, and sleep beforehand during the day if he can.
Pele Yoetz 88:6: And the women too must strengthen themselves with much vigor and might to stand firm to hear the entire reading of the Haggadah in its proper form and to fulfill all the mitzvot practiced on this night in their proper form, for they too are obligated in everything just as the men are. And she shall not stand up in the middle of the reading of the Haggadah to prepare the food, for that would be a transgression on her part - therefore let her prepare everything beforehand, and let her ears be attentive to all the words of the Haggadah with affection. And if she becomes drowsy from being tired and weary, her husband shall wake her, and she shall exert herself by washing her face and the like, so as not to lose much good, and "according to the pain is the reward" (Avot end of ch. 5). And many of the common people do not do well who greatly shorten the reading of the Haggadah on the first night of Passover, running out hurried, and leave the lengthening for the second night - for the essential mitzvah of the telling of the Exodus from Egypt applies only on the first night, as is known, and the second night is only by their own [Rabbinic] words, on account of the custom of our fathers in our hands. And although the matter is ancient and there is a complete obligation, nevertheless the essential Torah-mandated mitzvah is on the first night - therefore one must strengthen himself and make it his main effort to lengthen it more on the first night. The weak shall say, I am mighty, to fulfill a matter in its proper time - how good this is, and the LORD shall grant the good.
Pele Yoetz 89:1: Arousal - Arousal is a great principle in the Torah, and this is the whole of man: that he set his heart to be aroused to fear and to love and to fulfill every good thing in its proper form, as is fitting to do, and to withdraw his hand from doing any evil. But what shall the son do who has nothing to arouse him to arousal, and the evil inclination casts a deep sleep upon a person and does not let him become aroused? But for everything there is a remedy, and one shall wage war with stratagems - for at the time when the evil inclination is present, one does not remember the good inclination; therefore, you too, forestall the wicked one before he forestalls you. And do as I have written under the entry "Fence" - that he write down for himself, for every matter, the arousal that is needed, and read it, or [read] in the books that speak of that matter - if it is something that applies every day, let him read the arousal every single day, and if it is something that applies only from time to time, let him read the arousal close to its time, and a matter in its proper time, how good. And it is good for a man to teach or tell the members of his household the arousal needed for each matter in its proper time, for by bringing the words out of his mouth with a broadened, learned tongue, and making them understand what this mitzvah is and how it is fitting to perform it and what reason there is in it, and likewise in this manner what this transgression is and how severe it is and how it is fitting to distance oneself from it - he too shall add knowledge and shall add arousal and shall strengthen himself more and more; "much have I learned from my teachers," and so on, "and from my students more than all of them" (Ta'anit 7a). And it is also good for a man to make an external arousal to indicate love and fear and great joy and the like, a matter in its proper time as needed, so that it be recognizable in the expression of his face and the movement of his body - to whatever extent there is no concern of the mockery of mockers or appearing as arrogance, so shall he do and so shall he continue, for external arousal arouses and also brings about internal arousal.
Pele Yoetz 89:2: However, arousal benefits one who is alive but asleep - when they arouse him and say to him, "son of man, why are you dozing? Awaken and arise," then he shall awaken from his sleep and do his duty. But one who is dead, arousal does not benefit him, for the flesh of the dead does not feel the scalpel. So too in this matter: one whom the fear of the LORD has touched his heart, but his inclination has overpowered him and led him astray from his own mind and from the mind of his Maker, until after many days that thing has become to him like something permitted through habit - then, when arousal comes to him through his study of ethics books or hearing them taught, his heart shall be aroused and shall tremble within him, and he shall regret completely and seek a remedy for his illness, and shall return and be healed for himself. Not so the wicked, who have sunk so deeply in the mire of transgressions that the fear of the LORD is not before their faces at all, for due to the impurity of their sins the splendor of the Shechinah has grown very distant from them, "and the unclean spirit will I cause to pass out of the land," and their sins have multiplied - and due to their habituation, these things have become to them as permitted, and their own way is straight in their eyes. Of such men our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 18b): the wicked, in their lifetimes, are called dead. And then, not only does he not become aroused of himself at all, but even if he hears, from time to time, some arousal from the mouth of books or from the mouth of authors, he neither cares nor feels it - in one ear the words enter and out the other ear they exit, and there is almost no remedy for them, and the gates of repentance are locked before them, for how shall they repent since their own way is straight in their eyes and their heart is not aroused at all to seek out their own iniquity, hating and despising the wise and doubting the words of our holy Rabbis, of blessed memory - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yalkut Shimoni, beginning of Parashat Bechukotai, and Rashi brought it in Parashat Bechukotai), that seven transgressions - the first drags the second, until the seventh: since he does not study, he does not perform [mitzvot], and since he does not perform, he despises others who do perform, for he wishes that the evil of the many be the comfort of fools, and afterward he hates the wise and prevents others [from studying], and gives support to transgressors, and denies the mitzvot, and denies the fundamental principle [of faith]. Behold, therefore, no light shines upon them, and in darkness they walk until the day of their death, and forever they labor and run toward the pit of destruction with none to heal them.
Pele Yoetz 89:3: Only this remedy have we found: if he can subdue his inclination to study or to hear teachings constantly, day by day and night by night, even against his will and not for his own good - "it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it," and "whoever occupies himself with it idly, it gives him life," and it is written (Deuteronomy 32:2), "my teaching shall drip like rain." Just as raindrops eventually bore through stone, so the Torah eventually bores through the heart of stone and removes the heart of stone, and a proper spirit shall be renewed within him - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sukkah 52b): draw it to the study house; if it is stone, it shall dissolve; if it is iron, it shall shatter. But great diligence is needed, and after many days he shall find a remedy and shall feel within himself how his soul has come to life for him.
Pele Yoetz 89:4: And there is yet another remedy: if Heaven assists him that it happens upon him to perform a great mitzvah, then "the commandment of the LORD is pure" shall be his helpers, and it shall cause the LORD to dig for him a tunnel beneath the throne of glory to bring him back in repentance, and suddenly a proper spirit shall be renewed within him, and his heart shall be aroused and his soul shall be inflamed, and he shall repent completely, and shall walk in a straight path until all who know and recognize him shall say, "he is a different person." And they have already told a story (and it seems to me it is found in the Midrash) that once there was a wicked man who left no transgression untransgressed, and he went to a sage as though mocking, and said to him: is there any remedy for me? Before the sage lay a coal saved from a fire. He said to him: when this coal bears fruit, you shall have a remedy. And after some days passed, the sage saw the coal, and a blossom had sprouted and a bud had budded. And he sent to summon that man, and said to him: what have you done, that the LORD desires you? See the coal I spoke of to you. And he told him that it had happened to him that he came upon a man who was digging after the grave of a young woman who had died, in order to remove her from her grave for lustful purposes, and he was jealous with the zeal of the LORD of hosts and drew his sword and killed him. He said to him: that is what benefited you. And he turned back and became a complete penitent. And the masters of ethics have already written that when arousal for something comes to a person, he shall immediately seize it and hold fast to it and not let it go, and shall hasten to do it before its heat cools, and one mitzvah draws another mitzvah, so that its taste may endure, and the LORD shall be with him.
Pele Yoetz 90:1: Rendering Halachic Decisions - Well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Sotah 22a), on the verse (Proverbs 7:26), "for she has cast down many wounded" - this refers to a Torah scholar who has not reached the level of rendering decisions yet renders them; "and numerous are all her slain" - this refers to a Torah scholar who has reached the level of rendering decisions yet does not render them. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 145b?[adapted]), on the verse (Proverbs 7:4), "say to wisdom, you are my sister" - if the matter is as clear to you as your sister, who is forbidden to you, state it; and if not, do not state it. And this was said in the Talmud even regarding matters that have no practical legal consequence whatsoever - all the more so when there is practical legal consequence. And not only that, but there is a concern that he might permit the forbidden or purify the impure - then let the man tremble and be seized, and let it seem to him as though a sword lay between his loins and Gehinnom were open beneath him, and let him not bring forth from his mouth to say "permitted" or "pure" until the matter is as clear to him as the sun, and let him not rely on his memory, but rather examine the matter in a book at the time of the act, lest his memory be false. And if he cannot find the matter explicitly stated to be lenient, let him not rely on his own knowledge to render a lenient decision through his own dialectical reasoning, even if he is a great sage in the eyes of all the people - let him not be ashamed to ask other sages, for "two are better than one" (Ecclesiastes 4:9), and every man is a liar, and "according to the difficulty is the error" (Bava Metzia 96b).
Pele Yoetz 90:2: And they have already said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 7b) that when Rava had a case of a torn animal [regarding kashrut] come before him, he would gather all the butchers of Mechoza, saying: this is so that a share of the responsibility reaches them - meaning, so that a portion reaches them from the wooden beam [i.e., is shared among them], so that if I err in judgment, the whole burden of the punishment shall not be upon me alone, but shall be borne among all of us, and it shall be lightened for me. And we, orphans of orphans, what shall we answer after him? Therefore, if the matter is not explicit in the books, he shall not render a lenient ruling until he has discussed and consulted with other sages. And even to be stringent requires great deliberation, for if it is something permitted and he forbids it, how many evils does he cause! First, it is possible that there are holy sparks in that food which were destined to be repaired, and it turns out that he is a destroyer of souls. Furthermore, it turns out that he robs the owner of the item, causing him a loss. And if he declares the pure to be impure [ritually, regarding a woman], his evil is great, for perhaps, God forbid, he may cause her husband to come to the transgression of seminal emission for naught. Therefore every wise-hearted person, when a halachic decision comes before him, shall tremble greatly and his heart shall be humbled, and he shall lift his eyes on high and say, "for Your salvation I have hoped, O LORD," and he shall examine thoroughly, thoroughly, to the extent of his ability. So too in monetary law, which is a great section of the Torah, he shall tremble greatly to remove money from the possession of the one holding it unless the matter is as clear as the sun, or until he has discussed the halachah with other sages.
Pele Yoetz 90:3: And I have already written elsewhere another remedy for this: that the straight path is that in every city they appoint deputies to stand at the right hand of the local halachic authority, and they should not decide matters strictly according to Torah law but rather according to what is proper, by a compromise close to the law. (And all that is said on this matter, and more, under the entry "Judgment and Law," is not intended for those who sit on seats of judgment - for what do I know that they do not know? And certainly whoever enters this arena must first study the laws of judgments as is proper to do; rather, let these words of mine be for myself, as a remembrance between my eyes, and for men of lesser standing like myself - I intend them not as one who warns, but as one who reminds.) And let him always precede with prayer and pour out his soul before the LORD that he not stumble in a matter of halachah and that nothing improper come forth from under his hand. And certainly "a judge has only what his eyes see" (Bava Batra 131a), and "the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures" (Avodah Zarah 3a) - rather, let him do what is in his power to do and investigate to the extent of his ability, and if he cannot find the matter clear and has no one to ask, and must render a practical halachic decision immediately, let him go toward stringency and choose the lesser evil, for it is better to forbid the permitted than to permit the forbidden. And in a place where there are other men who can judge and render decisions, he should not wish nor consent to sit at the head, even if he needs a livelihood and is great in wisdom and in number of years - even so, let him flee from the rabbinate and cast his burden upon the LORD, and He shall sustain him, and let him leave greatness to whoever desires it, and let him spare himself from judgment, for great is the evil of the rabbinate (as I shall write under the entry "Judgment"). But in a place where there are no [qualified] men, let a man strive to bring merit to the many and rely on the mercy of Heaven for the sake of the many.
Pele Yoetz 91:1: Kindling - Kindling constitutes a mitzvah (Shabbat 22b) with Sabbath candles and Chanukah candles (as I shall write under the entry "Ner" [candle]). And kindling lamps in the synagogue is also a mitzvah, as it is written (Isaiah 24:15), "in the lights, glorify the LORD." However, I have already stated that a person must choose between the good and the better, and one who does not have so much surplus wealth as to fulfill both this and that - in a place where he would give candles and oil to a synagogue where, without his giving, there would be no lack, for there is no poor congregation, and this is somewhat comparable to casting water into the sea - and granted that he performs a mitzvah in that the mitzvah is performed with his money, it is nevertheless better if he gives those candles and that oil to a worthy poor person, or to a Torah scholar, who shall kindle the Sabbath candle or study by their light. Therefore, even on a yahrzeit day, let him do so, for according to the greatness of the mitzvah, so does it add to giving peace of mind to the souls of his parents - unless he does it for the honor of the living and the dead and so that people not gossip about him, for not everyone knows that it is better to act according to the law. But he should not multiply kindlings if his means do not extend so far. And charity is greater than sacrifices (Beit HaMidrash, Jellinek, vol. 3), all the more so than kindling in the synagogue - provided he sets aside the money he would have wished to give for oil and candles, and buys oil and candles, and gives to Torah scholars and to the poor beyond what he had intended to distribute as charity - and this shall be good for the LORD and for the soul of his parents.
Pele Yoetz 91:2: But if he is a poor man, his own life and the life of the members of his household take precedence, and it is better that he buy oil and candles for himself so that he may have the means to kindle the Sabbath candle and study by its light, and it shall be counted as charity for him more than if he gave to the synagogue. And everything depends on what kind of person he is - if the LORD has widened his borders, this is his honor, for he increases the honor of the synagogue, and "in lights the LORD shall be honored," and through this he shall merit the candle of mitzvah and Torah as light for himself and his descendants. And I have seen men of deeds who cherished the kindling of the synagogue's candles and would not allow it to be done by the synagogue attendant, but rather they themselves, with their own honor, would kindle them. And I have heard that there are places where they sell the kindling [as an honor], and certainly this is a cherishing of the mitzvah and a fine custom. And well known is their saying, of blessed memory (Yerushalmi, Shevi'it, end of ch. 3), that Saul merited the kingship on account of the merit of his grandfather, who would kindle lights in the dark alleyways and perform kindness with the multitude; and likewise Deborah merited prophecy because she was diligent in making thick wicks for the Temple (Yalkut Shimoni, Judges, remez 4). Let the wise man hear and add learning, and let him do what is in his power to do good, and the LORD shall grant the good. And how good and how pleasant it is for one whose borders the LORD has widened, that a candle burn for him all night (in a room where he does not use his bed), for this is great preparation for standing in early rising, since much of the incitement of the evil inclination comes from laziness to light the candle. Behold, therefore, it shall be counted as an expenditure for a mitzvah, and the LORD shall repay him with his own [reward], peace be in his rampart.
Pele Yoetz 92:1: "Yes" is Righteousness - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 113a): let your "yes" be righteousness and your "no" be righteousness. And Rav said to Rav Kahana (ibid.): turn over carcasses [i.e., take on menial work] rather than turn over your words. And it is fitting for a person to have within him something of the knowledge of his Maker, that for good He does not retract, but for evil He does retract. So too shall the good man do: if he uttered from his mouth to do good with his fellow, or not to do him harm, he shall not retract in any manner or for any reason in the world, for it is a great shame - but if he uttered from his mouth to do evil or not to do a kindness, he shall not stand by his word. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Eruvin 65b): whoever is placated by his wine has in him something of the knowledge of his Maker, as it is written (Genesis 8:21), "and the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma." Rashi explained: whoever is placated by his wine - when he drinks a little wine, he regrets the evil due to the cheerfulness of his mind, and when they appease him, he is appeased - has in him something of the knowledge of his Maker, for through the offering that Noah offered, the LORD regretted the evil and swore not to bring a flood upon the world again. And it is written (Exodus 32:14), "and the LORD regretted the evil that He had spoken of doing to His people."
Pele Yoetz 92:2: And were it not for the LORD of hosts, He would have reverted from the attribute of punishment to a good attribute - "we would have perished, we would have been lost," God forbid - and every good thing that comes forth from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, even conditionally, does not retract. And granted we find it written (Genesis 32:8), "and Jacob was greatly afraid," and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 4a) that even though He had said to him, "and I will guard you wherever you go" (ibid. 28:15), he feared lest sin cause [the promise to be withheld]. And likewise our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 33a) that whoever disgraces his mouth [with vulgar speech] - even if a decree of seventy good years had been sealed upon him, it is overturned upon him for evil. And so too we find regarding the destruction of the Temple, that He reversed [a promise] and said (Ezekiel 9:6), "and from My sanctuary you shall begin" - meaning "from My sanctified ones you shall begin" (Shabbat 55a). The interpretation of the matter is that He never reverses a good decree for evil, and the word of our God which He has spoken good concerning Israel shall stand forever, and we shall receive the good without any doubt in the world, for His reasoning is good - but at a given moment sin may cause it to be overturned for evil, for his own benefit and his own good, for "whatever the Merciful One does, He does for good," for it is good for a man that they should do it to him, "for better one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world" (Avot 4:17). And likewise if it appears to a person that in doing the good he said he would do for his fellow, harm would come to his fellow from another side, or to another person, then indeed permission is granted for him to retract, for this is like a case of retracting from evil.
Pele Yoetz 92:3: And now there are many who have this trait, that they stand by their word in everything, and their reward comes out at their own loss - for they act this way even for evil, or when they have said they will not do good; even if friends multiply against him [pleading with him to change], he shall not retract, and he shall say, "my words - it is impossible that two [outcomes] be made of them, and the utterance of my lips I shall not change, even if they gave me all the treasures of the world." Such a man is bad company, and he distances from himself both friend and companion, and his enemies multiply, and hatred and rivalry increase against him, and even in his own home he shall have no peace, and even the members of his own household are not accepted by him, since he says forever, "as I have said, so must it be," and my word shall not return empty. This is a bad, sick trait, causing every illness.
Pele Yoetz 92:4: And this is the teaching of the good man: that he retract and nullify his own opinion in deference to the opinion of others, according to the need of the hour, and that he be appeased through mercy and be reconciled through supplications. And he shall always deliberate greatly before uttering from his mouth to do a good thing for his fellow, or not to do him evil - but once he has uttered it with his mouth, "that which has gone out of his lips he shall keep and shall do," and shall not transgress it. And therefore it is better that he first say he will not do good and then retract [and do it], than that he say he will do it and then retract [and not do it] - for "to speak and then go back is folly and shame for him." And on the other hand, he should not turn away his fellow's word empty-handed, and should not contradict his fellow's words as much as he can, even if he is his enemy, in order to fulfill (Psalms 34:15), "seek peace and pursue it." And not like many quarrelsome people who say, "I do not care to do this" - just so that it not be said that he acted according to his friend's word and did not have his own way - this is the trait of Sodom, and it is not fitting to act this way except with one's own young children, in order to train and teach them not to have this bad trait of holding fast and insisting on their own way and not budging from their own knowledge. But with all other people, and even with one's own grown children, it is good for a man not to insist on his own opinion, and to let the elders be heeded by the younger ones, in order to increase love and brotherhood, peace and friendship. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ta'anit 20b): a person should always be soft like a reed and not hard like a cedar. And through this, for an everlasting remembrance, "the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon."
Pele Yoetz 93:1: Diverting the Mind - This is a great principle regarding solitary devotion: that he not divert his mind from all the things that are obligations of the body and obligations of the heart. And if it happens that he diverts his mind, when he remembers his Holy Rock he shall return - may He have mercy on him - let him seize it and not let it go; so shall he do, even coming and going repeatedly, let him remember what his obligation is and hasten to do it. And I have already stated that the great fence against diverting one's mind is writing, for sight brings about remembrance. And especially regarding tefillin, extra caution is needed not to divert one's mind from them, for the very purpose of the Creator, blessed be His Name, in commanding them is as a remembrance of what is written in them and the benefit that follows from it, toward fear and love and the like, for upon this depends the essential fulfillment of the mitzvah of tefillin, and the intention of the heart is thereafter the essence of the matter (and I have already written under the entry "Heart" some things that are obligations of the heart which it is fitting for a person not to divert his mind from). And likewise, if he received any benefit at all from his fellow, it is fitting that he not forget it and not divert it from his mind. Correspondingly, if his fellow did him a great evil, he shall forget it and divert it from his mind, to fulfill what the Torah said (Leviticus 19:18), "you shall not bear a grudge." And likewise, when foreign thoughts and evil ruminations come to his mind, and especially during prayer and Torah study and the service of the blessed Name, let him divert them from his mind, and let a man muster his strength to divert them from his mind and turn his heart to words of Torah or to the service of the blessed Name, and let his heart be toward our Father in Heaven, and let him cry out and say, "save me, my Lord the King, rescue me from the mire and let me not sink" - perhaps his Maker will have mercy on him.
Pele Yoetz 93:2: And likewise our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 75a): worry in a person's heart, he should divert it from his mind. Especially at a time of joy and at a time of the service of the blessed Name, he must settle his mind, and through deep pure thoughts and with the help of the Almighty he shall find sufficient arguments to divert from his mind whatever needs to be diverted from his mind. And since a person's mind cannot think two thoughts at once, when one of these thoughts that needs to be diverted comes to him, let him exchange it and replace the evil with good. And if he cannot accomplish this alone, they said regarding this (ibid.): let him tell it to others - let him go to a sage and tell him his distress, and he shall teach him understanding so that he may awaken from his sleep and not remain drowsy, and the waters of the river shall not be turned to blood, but rather he shall manage his affairs with judgment, for this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 94:1: Striking - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Moed Katan 17a): one who strikes his grown son is liable to be placed under a ban. And by the same reasoning we too shall learn that it is not specifically a grown son, for the reason is because it causes his son to kick against him and treat his father with contempt, and it turns out that he transgresses "and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14). Behold, therefore, it is not necessarily a truly grown son, but even a young one, whenever it is known about him that he does not accept authority - such as in generations of insolence, where insolence increases and a son kicks against his father, not through striking alone, but even if he rebukes him in anger, he too shall become angry and shall not accept the rebuke. And truly they said (Proverbs 17:10), "a rebuke enters deeper into a man of understanding than a hundred blows into a fool" - "into a man of understanding," they said, but one who does not understand does not accept rebuke. And there is a son who does not obey the voice of his father and the voice of his mother, and for all such cases, understanding is needed on the part of the father and mother, who know and recognize their children, that they are difficult and that the fear of the LORD is not before their faces and they do not obey the voice of their father and mother - let them not command them to do anything to serve them, and let them strive not to become angry at them and not to rebuke them, and let them speak to them only in a gentle language. And granted that not all times are alike, and there are times when father and mother cannot restrain themselves from commanding their children anything and from becoming angry at them and reproaching and cursing them, for their teeth grind and their heart melts upon seeing their children do things that are not proper - nevertheless, whatever is in their power to do, let them do, and let them choose the lesser evil.
Pele Yoetz 94:2: And behold, the will of father and mother is to bring merit to the souls of their children, that they do the will of their father and mother and thereby bring merit to their own souls by giving peace of mind to their Former. But what shall they do when the generation is not so favorable, and as long as the sons and daughters are with their father and mother they do not desire this mitzvah so much and do not value them so much - but when they go to the Land of Israel or to their eternal home, then they shall say, "who will give me a father and mother, that I may lick the dust of their feet and carry them and bear them and serve them with all my strength?" But if they wish that the LORD count it for them as though they had done it, so let them do it while they have the ability to do it, and then a good thought, when they cannot act on it, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins it to the deed. And according to these generations, children of ascent who obey the voice of their father and mother are few, and especially when they marry wives, where the daughter-in-law quarrels with her mother-in-law and it is difficult for the reality to conform to proper honor - how good and how pleasant it would be for father and mother, if it is possible for them, to separate their children so that they are not dependent upon their table; and it is likewise good for the children, if it is with the will of their father and mother, that they separate from their table, for the absence [of contact] is better than the presence of evil. And would that it be the heart of the children to honor their father and mother and receive good reward, fruits, in this world, so that they too shall be honored by their own good children, with the principal remaining for the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 94:3: And the prohibition against striking is not only regarding one's own son, but also regarding all other people there is the prohibition of "he shall not add [to strike], lest he add [more strokes]" (Makkot 23a). And they have already said (Sanhedrin 58b): one who slaps his fellow's cheek is as though he slapped the cheek of the Shechinah. And Rashi explained: one who strikes on the cheek. And the same law applies everywhere, only they spoke of the common case. And it is written, "the arm of the exalted shall be broken" (Job 38:15), and "the man of the arm, to him belongs the land" (ibid. 22:8), and Rav Huna cut off a hand (Sanhedrin ibid.). And it is likewise fitting for all leaders of cities to chastise men of violence, and especially the worthless men who strike their wives with cruel blows - may the spirit of those who do these things be blasted, who treat the daughters of Israel like maidservants, trampling and striking and having relations with them without any shame, and it is fitting for whoever has the ability to chastise them as much as they can, and if they can remove their wives from under their hand, if it is with the woman's own will - for no woman dwells with a serpent in one place - it is a great mitzvah to rescue the oppressed from the hand of their oppressor.
Pele Yoetz 94:4: And even to strike small children, no person has permission except a father toward his sons, and a teacher toward his students, and a guardian appointed over the young. And even a teacher toward his students - it is written in responsa (Hilchot Ketanot, part 1, siman 125) that it would have been fitting to appoint a court to strike them in proper measure and proportion, except that this was not the practice. And it is found in the Talmud (Bava Batra 21a) that Rav said to Rav Shmuel bar Shilat: when you strike a child, strike only with a shoelace, so that whoever heeds shall heed [i.e., a light punishment suffices for the obedient]. And so it is found in Sefer Chasidim (siman 49) that no one has permission to strike except a teacher toward his students. And it is likewise found in the responsa of Maharashdam (Orach Chaim, siman 20) that if one struck a minor and was brought to judgment for it, they take up his case and fix a fine for him. And I recall a certain God-fearing man who was a guardian over children, that at the time of his death he commanded that it be announced in the synagogue that he asks forgiveness from all the children if he struck any of them improperly - for certainly, even regarding one's own young sons and one's students, the strap was not permitted for striking them improperly, for no violence in their hands [i.e., though they did nothing wrong], and even if there is a need to strike them, there is no permission to strike them a great blow, a cruel blow, on the head or on the eye, a place where one could cause a blemish or endanger life, God forbid - but rather he shall strike them gently on the legs, without anger. And this is a great principle: for a good man manages his affairs in judgment, in measure, in weight, and in proportion - this is the straight path.
Pele Yoetz 95:1: Clothing - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 14a): the Holy One, blessed be He, clothes the naked - you too shall clothe the naked, as it is written (Genesis 3:21), "and the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skin, and clothed them." And it is written (Isaiah 58:7-8), "when you see the naked, that you cover him... then your light shall break forth like the dawn," and so on. And truly it is a necessity and a great obligation to have mercy on the poor regarding the matter of clothing even more than regarding food, for regarding food one can economize and be content with little, and a man can go out to his work and labor all day and earn two coins and buy bread to eat at night and be satisfied with bread and be well, and he does not need people's help so much - not so regarding the matter of clothing, which requires much money at once, and the poor man's hand cannot reach it, for even to eat to satisfaction he has not enough, and so his situation continually worsens, and his garments become tear upon tear and patch upon patch, until nothing remains for him but a single shirt and a garment of tattered rags, in a manner that his life is not truly life - and it is fitting for the children of Israel, compassionate ones, children of compassionate ones, that their hearts stir and be filled with compassion for them.
Pele Yoetz 95:2: And the man whom the LORD has graced with wealth and honor - such shall be his practice: that he make for himself and for all the members of his household new garments for each festival, from head to foot, and give his worn-out garments to worthy poor people, and especially to Torah scholars, who must maintain a dignified bearing and for whom it is not befitting their honor to wear tattered rags and torn, patched garments - one must have mercy on them all the more. And through this a rich man shall glory in his wealth. And what appears to the rich man as despised, disgraceful, and worn out is, to the poor man, valuable and exalted. And it is true that Scripture states (Numbers 18:30), "when you have set apart the best of it," and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Temurah 5a[?]) that one must set apart the choicest, most praiseworthy, and finest portion - all according to what kind of person one is, for they said (Bava Metzia 62a), "your life takes precedence" - he himself takes precedence to wear the new garment, and the old shall be removed on account of the new. However, it is good for a man to be exacting, if he can discern and know whether the recipient of a gift considers it important and dear and needful to him. And if it happens that they gave to a poor man some garment of tattered rags that is not at all dear to him, he should not complain against the rich man nor speak disparagingly of him before others, for this causes the door to be locked before the rich from giving their worn-out garments to the poor. And it is the way of a good man who has proper and settled understanding, that whenever his fellow thinks to do him a favor and buys him something, even if it is a poor item and he bought it dearly, and likewise if he gives him a gift of lesser things, he shall show him a pleasant face and hold it in great regard for him, as though this item were greatly needed and dear and pleasant and agreeable - for by this his mind shall be at ease, and the door shall not be locked before doers of kindness - this is the way of the good.
Pele Yoetz 95:3: And behold, there are many places accustomed to clothing the children of the poor, dressing them from Chanukah to Chanukah - happy are they, how good is their portion, for they perform a great mitzvah. But would that their heart and their ability allow them to do so also for the poor who are adults, and their wives and their young children. Let the weak say, "I am mighty," for this mitzvah, for it is great - it shall shield them, leaving blessing and success upon all the works of their hands, wealth and riches in their houses, and in the World to Come they shall eat the fruit of their righteousness; they shall carry a blessing from the LORD and from the wretched poor; their offspring shall be mighty in the land, and they shall leave their surplus to their children.
Pele Yoetz 96:1: Lending - It is known that this is one of the 613 mitzvot: to lend to whoever needs to borrow, whether to a poor man or to a rich man - except that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Metzia 71a): the poor and the rich - the poor takes precedence. And even between lending to a gentile with interest and lending to a Jew without interest, the Jew takes precedence (Tanchuma, Mishpatim, 14). And although in lending to a gentile with interest one also fulfills the mitzvah "to a foreigner you may lend with interest" (Deuteronomy 23:21), and he has the benefit of eating the fruits [i.e., the interest], the mitzvah of lending to a Jew surpasses these. For our Father, our Shepherd, does not desire our loss, and there is no restraint upon the LORD to pay the profit in this world manifold more than what the gentile gives. And it is possible that likewise, if a rich man wishes to take payment in a permissible manner by way of a business partnership, and a poor man wishes to borrow for free, the poor man takes precedence, and all the more so, since in taking payment from a Jew there is no mitzvah at all - and even though the loan itself to a rich man is a mitzvah, it is possible that when he gives it for payment for his own benefit, there is not so much of a mitzvah, even if the rich man asked him to do him this kindness of lending to him for payment at his time of need. However, it seems that everything depends on the need: if the poor man wishes to borrow to buy some superfluous item that he could do without, and the rich man wishes to pay off his creditor so as not to come to shame, disgrace, and humiliation, and so as not to lose his credit (such as in the payment of a promissory note ["polisa"]) - at that time, birth pangs come upon the rich man - in such a case certainly the rich man takes precedence, for he is, at that moment, more of a "poor man" than all the poor.
Pele Yoetz 96:2: And certainly it was not said that just as with a gentile for payment and a Jew for free the Jew takes precedence, this applies to one whose borders the LORD has widened and who has another place to earn his living, and does not lend to a gentile with interest except to fulfill the mitzvah "to a foreigner you may lend with interest" - then the mitzvah of lending to a Jew takes precedence. But if he needs to take payment for his own livelihood, they have already said, "his own life takes precedence." However, the difficulty is that now people have found an opening to say that now everyone needs it for his own livelihood, and "he who loves money shall not be satisfied with money" (Ecclesiastes 5:9), and he finds for himself an excusing argument to say that he is unable to lend for free - but shall not God search this out, for He knows whether he is able or not able? And since human nature seeks good for itself and its eye is evil regarding its own possessions, the Torah was therefore stringent in its warning and wrote (Deuteronomy 15:9), "beware lest there be a base thought in your heart, saying, the seventh year, the year of release, approaches, and your eye be evil against your needy brother." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Bava Batra 10a) that he is considered like one who worships idols - it is written here "base" (beliya'al) and it is written there (Judges 19:22), "certain base fellows went out." And due to the severity of this, let the man tremble and be seized. And according to what is written there, "the seventh year approaches," we may learn that even if there is room for concern about monetary loss, he should not refrain from lending, and the LORD shall repay him.
Pele Yoetz 96:3: And certainly everything depends on what kind of person one is, and it is known that for everything, even a good thing and a trait of piety, there is a limit and a measure, and a scale and just balances are needed so as not to tilt to either of the two extremes, but rather a complete middle path - as we learned (Avot 2:1): which is the straight path? Whichever is honor to the one who does it and honor to him from mankind. And the sage already said (Chovot HaLevavot, Introduction): part of caution is that one not be overly cautious - all the more so in this matter, of which it is said (Psalms 112:5), "good is the man who is gracious and lends, he manages his affairs with judgment." And certainly it is not good to act in a manner that his capital would be entirely depleted and he could not continue doing good and would himself need the help of others - rather, this is the straight path that a person should choose: that if the LORD has graced him with wealth and possessions beyond the need of his livelihood, he shall set aside a portion of his possessions as the LORD's blessing given to him, or if he has the good practice of setting aside a tithe from his earnings, a portion of it he shall keep aside to lend as gracious and kind loans - and this shall be an enduring fund for him to perform this mitzvah all the days of his life, and even after his death he shall not be free of the mitzvot, and his righteousness shall stand forever, and his righteousness shall go before him and after him.
Pele Yoetz 96:4: And if he cannot do this in his lifetime, let him at least remember while he is still alive not to leave all his wealth to others and leave his own soul bare, and let him not rely on his sons' table that they will send him the fruit of their righteousness - but rather let him make a proper will, in a beneficial manner, so that at least a tenth of his estate, or some portion of his possessions, shall remain for himself as an enduring fund in the hands of a trustworthy person, close to gain and far from loss, to perform charity and loans. And it is even better if he sets aside some land for this purpose, for land endures forever. And how sweet and pleasant it shall be for him, each time his righteousness follows after him and he eats the fruit of his deeds - then he shall give thanks for his portion and shall regret not having done more. And for this too, a scale and just balances are needed: if his sons are Torah scholars and poor, they take precedence, to have mercy on them as a father has mercy on his children, and to strengthen their hands so that they stand guard over Torah and over service.
Pele Yoetz 96:5: And when he comes to lend, let him uphold the words of the Sages, who said (Bava Metzia 75b) that whoever lends to his fellow without witnesses transgresses "before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14) and brings a curse upon himself. Therefore, he should not proceed with any loan, whether in money or in merchandise, without making a document with witnesses, or a handwritten note with full legal force, so that it be considered like a formal document and that he may collect through it even from the property of orphaned minors, and not worry about the scribe's fee, or he should learn to write it himself - for many times an impure incident occurs where he cannot collect his debt because he has no document or handwritten note, and then his teeth shall grind and melt, and he shall cry out with no one to save him, and it would serve him right to lose his money for having transgressed the words of the Sages. And if he comes to lend to a man who is not so trustworthy, he should lend to him only against a pledge - and it is even better if he practices this with everyone, even someone trustworthy, so as not to shame the one who is not trustworthy and not to cause jealousy and hatred. Therefore it is better that all who know him recognize that he does not lend without a pledge, even to the king, all the more so since one does not know what a day may bring, and how many people have lain down rich and risen from their beds poor. Therefore they said: a pledge in the house, peace in the house. And if the borrower is a rich man, he may take from him a small amount of profit to add to the principal of his loans, but to a poor man he shall lend for free, gracious and kind loans. And if he knows that the borrower has nothing to pledge against the loan, let him at least ask him for a good guarantor.
Pele Yoetz 96:6: And if he knows about him that he cannot even find a guarantor, then, if he asks him for an amount that, if he were to lose it, he could bear, and the borrower has a presumption of being a good man and has a place to earn so that he can repay his debt if he wishes - then let him lend to him once on his trustworthiness. But he should not give him debt upon debt until he pays off the first one, and then, may He have mercy on us, [he may lend him] that same amount again - but he should not rely on his trustworthiness to keep lending him more and more, for there are cheats who commonly repay four or five times until they are considered trustworthy, and then they are given much, and then they consume the lender's money as well. Therefore he should not increase [the loan] and should give him only that same amount, even on the condition that he might lose it. But to a man he considers a cheat, he should not lend at all without a pledge - and so that his own inclination not lead him to consider everyone a cheat and not to lend to anyone without a pledge, thereby locking the door before borrowers (for on the whole it is not so possible to borrow and give a pledge to the point that one is prevented from borrowing) - therefore let him test this: whether he truly suspects the person of being a cheat, or whether this is the counsel of his own [evil] inclination. Let him picture to himself, between himself and his Maker, in truth: if this man had come to him to borrow for payment and good profit, would he have trusted him and lent to him? Then let him reckon the reward of the mitzvah against the payment and profit the borrower would have given him, and trust him to lend to him for free even without a pledge. But if he would not have trusted him to lend to him even for payment, then he should not trust him without a pledge.
Pele Yoetz 96:7: And in any case, if he is a poor man and asks him for a small amount, even if it seems likely to him that he will not be able to repay, let him not turn him away crushed and ashamed, but rather give it to him on the understanding that he will not repay, in a manner that the borrower not be considered wicked when he fails to repay - for then he [the lender] transgresses "before the blind" - and it does not suffice that he forgive him in his heart, for in any case the borrower intends toward a prohibition, since it is not revealed to him that he has forgiven him. Rather, he must explicitly state his intention to him and say to him: do not be distressed that you cannot repay, for it does not matter to me, and I consider it as though I had already received it, and if the LORD widens your borders, then you shall repay me. And through this he shall merit two mitzvot: lending and charity, and the LORD shall repay him, as it is written (Psalms 37:21), "and the righteous is gracious and gives." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained: when a wicked man borrows and does not repay, the righteous lender is gracious and gives it as a gift, so as not to transgress "before the blind" and so that no person be punished on his account. Or alternatively, the Righteous One of the world is gracious and gives, and repays him the debt from another source, in a manner that he performs a mitzvah and knows nothing bad. And whoever is a proper Jew who believes with complete faith in these true words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, should not find it difficult in his eyes if he lent a sela to a poor man in his time of need and lost it - let him believe with complete faith that the LORD has already placed his money in his own purse with even greater increase, and his heart should not be grieved for his needy brother, and he should not lock the door before borrowers where it is proper to lend without a pledge, in the manner stated.
Pele Yoetz 96:8: However, when the loan amount is large and the man is not trustworthy, he should not lend without a pledge, so that he not come to regret the earlier ones, and he should not put him off with words, saying "go and come back, I will reconsider" - and likewise he should not act as the custom of certain rich men who think to perform generosity and charity, but instead of charity there is an outcry: when a poor man comes to entreat him to give him a loan of, for example, ten lira, and he is worried that the poor man will not repay him, he says, "here, take two lira as a gift, and leave the rest as straw for you" - and he does two evils thereby. First, he does not give him enough for his need, and the poor man would have preferred that he give him the ten as a loan rather than relieve his own conscience by giving him two as a gift - for after the effort of scheming until he removed the mask of shame from his face to come and entreat this rich man, in the end he shall leave utterly disappointed, and it shall be very distressing to him as he wonders where to turn for help - if this one, whom he thought it likely would fulfill his request, acted this way, how shall he go elsewhere? And a further sickening evil is that by giving him these two lira as a gift, he locks the door before the poor man, so that he will not come to him again to ask for a loan, for he will say, "now the rich man will think I am demanding by mouth that he give me more as a gift, since I now know this is his way."
Pele Yoetz 96:9: Behold, therefore, the good is truly good: when he cannot fulfill the poor man's wish, let him tell him explicitly that his means do not extend to it at that time, and appease him with words and satisfy his hungry soul, saying to him, "as my soul lives, I grieve for you, my brother, and I would wish to help you with all my soul, but what can I do, since my means do not extend to it?" And if he has the means but does not wish to give without a pledge, let him tell him explicitly to bring a pledge and he will lend to him. And if he does not wish to press the poor man, he may vary his words and say to him, "I have none myself, but if you wish, bring me a pledge and I will seek [a loan] for you from my friends." And if he does not wish to lend to him at all, he should not give him charity at that moment instead, for then "the sword comes forth" as stated above.
Pele Yoetz 96:10: And when he lends against a pledge, let him spell out his terms in writing, signed by the borrower's hand, that if he does not repay him by the appointed time, he shall be permitted to sell the pledge without the court's permission and even in a discount market, and that the pledge shall be at the borrower's own risk, and that he [the lender] shall be believed on his own simple word regarding whatever he says. And all such matters he should spell out in an explicit document, so that evil not befall him instead of good, and he not come to regret the good deed, God forbid, and so that people not have complaints against him. And the good way is that he entrust that portion of money he has set aside for this purpose into the hand of a third party, and instruct him to conduct himself in this manner - not to give without a pledge and without an explicit document as stated - and then there is no room for complaint, for the agent performs his agency and is not permitted to deviate. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Yevamot 63a) that whoever lends a sela to a poor man in his time of need, of him Scripture says (Isaiah 58:9), "then you shall call and the LORD shall answer, you shall cry and He shall say, here I am." And the commentators explained that they mean at the time of the lender's own difficulty - that even though at that time he himself is pressed for money, he shall press himself further to lend to the poor man.
Pele Yoetz 96:11: And the mitzvah of lending is not only in money but also in merchandise. If he gives to him on credit and does not add to the price of the item to charge him more expensively because it is on credit, he performs a mitzvah and builds a world of kindness. And since it is customary to give merchandise on credit even to a gentile, and it is not so difficult for him as lending money, a man can easily fulfill this great mitzvah, as it is written (Leviticus 25:35), "if your brother becomes poor and his hand falters, you shall strengthen him" - which is the greatest of charities - and he shall give it to him for less than what he sells to others, so that room remains for him to profit, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained on the verse (ibid. verse 14), "and if you sell a sale" - that he should give it to him in a manner that the buyer too shall have a sale and profit from it, and collect from him in small coins, little by little, for each coin joins to a great sum, and this can be the cause of his earning an honorable livelihood from the labor of his hands, and that he build up capital and even be able to reach the level of tithing, with the help of the Almighty. Of such a case it is said (Proverbs 21:21), "whoever pursues righteousness and kindness shall find life, righteousness, and honor." Nevertheless, it is good for a man to choose a manner of business in which he need not give on credit, for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sukkah 56b): better a scattered reading than one gathered - Rashi explained: better a little profit in hand than much on credit. And they said of a certain pious man that he would pray, "Merciful One, save me from scattering of the soul" - meaning, the scattering of his money, which is the scattering of the soul. And especially those who give to people in distant places and must set out on journeys that carry an element of danger in order to collect, and could instead say of themselves, "let us bring our own bread" - "better a dry morsel with peace in it" (Proverbs 17:1), and "the LORD's blessing, it enriches" (ibid. 10:22) - if it is decreed upon him to be rich, it is the one who increases [his own toil], not the one who does little; and the one who diminishes shall not lack."
Pele Yoetz 97:1: Halachah - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8a): from the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His world but the four cubits of halachah. And they said (ibid.): the LORD loves the gates that are distinguished through halachah. And there are two aspects to this, both of them equally good. The first is the study of halachah - that is, the Gemara through dialectical give-and-take, raising difficulties and resolving them - of this they said (Bava Metzia 33a): there is no measure better than Gemara, for instead of engaging in dialectics over other books and the words of the later authorities, it is better to engage in dialectics over the Gemara, for through the difficulties and their resolutions one separates the chaff from the wheat and adorns the "bride" (kallah), the letters of which spell "halachah." And of this they said: the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoices in dialectical give-and-take. Therefore it is fitting for every Torah scholar whose Torah is his profession to have a fixed time each day to study one halachah with intense dialectical analysis according to his ability. And if his own capacity does not extend to engaging in such wise dialectics, let him study the books of our commentator Rabbis who engage in this dialectic. And there is another explanation of "distinguished through halachah" - that they engage in dialectics to clarify the practical halachah and to bring forth a true judgment in its truth. This too is very good, to clarify doubtful legal questions.
